1                    I.      BACKGROUND AND SUMMARY

2    Q.   Please state your name, occupation, and business address.

3    A.   My name is Courtney Fieldman. I am the Utility Program Director at the

4         Southwest Energy Efficiency Project (“SWEEP”). My business address is

5         2334 Broadway, Suite A, Boulder, Colorado 80304.

6    Q.   For whom are you testifying?

7    A.   I am testifying on behalf of the Coalition for Clean Affordable Energy

 8        (“CCAE”).

 9   Q.   Please describe CCAE.

10   A.   CCAE is a coalition of twelve environmental and public interest groups

11        active in New Mexico and the broader Rocky Mountain and Southwest

12        region of the United States formed to promote clean and affordable energy

13        policies in New Mexico. To advance clean energy policy and programs in

14        New Mexico, CCAE uses strategically focused legal advocacy, scientific

15        analysis, and other strategies.

16   Q.   Please describe SWEEP.

17   A.   SWEEP is a regional nonprofit organization that advances energy

18        efficiency, demand-side management, beneficial electrification, demand

19        response, and related policies across the Southwest, including New Mexico.

20        SWEEP works to ensure that efficiency and flexibility resources are valued



                                            1
                        DOCKET NO. 25-00082-UT
              DIRECT TESTIMONY OF COURTNEY FIELDMAN

 1        and deployed in ways that reduce system costs, protect customers, and

 2        support a clean, reliable, and affordable electric system.

 3   Q.   What are your professional qualifications?

 4   A.   I am the Utility Program Director at SWEEP, where I lead legislative and

 5        regulatory strategy on data centers and large loads across six Southwest

 6        states,   including   intervention    in   utility   proceedings   involving

 7        interconnection, rate design, and demand-side resource valuation.

 8        Previously, I served as Building Electrification Associate at Rocky

 9        Mountain Institute, where I worked on building electrification policies in

10        Colorado, and I also held roles at the United Nations supporting the Paris

11        Agreement Global Stocktake. I hold a certificate from Harvard Business

12        School in Disruptive Innovation, a master’s in climate change law and

13        policy, and a bachelor’s degree from Princeton University. My statement of

14        qualifications is included as Exhibit CF-1.

15   Q.   What is the purpose of your testimony?

16   A.   In this rate case, El Paso Electric Company of New Mexico (“EPE” or the

17        “Company”) has asked the Commission to approve new tariffs and contracts

18        for data centers and a bill credit for low-income customers. I recommend

19        that the Commission not approve either proposal as filed and present

20        modifications that are in the public interest. Along with CCAE Witness Ron



                                            2
                        DOCKET NO. 25-00082-UT
              DIRECT TESTIMONY OF COURTNEY FIELDMAN

 1        Nelson’s testimony and recommendations, I believe that the Company’s

 2        large load proposals require additional customer protections.

 3                Additionally, I provide recommendations regarding the Company’s

 4        proposed low-income rate. As proposed, the low-income credit would be

 5        tied to the customer charge and credit the customer with only the monthly

 6        customer charge, the smallest part of the increase EPE requests in this case.

 7        I am also recommending that the Commission require the Company to

 8        modify the low-income credit so that it is not linked to the customer charge.

 9        The Commission should also require large load customers to pay an

10        Efficient Use of Energy Recovery Factor rider, with a portion of that

11        payment supporting low-income programs.

12          II.     EPE’S LARGE LOAD CUSTOMER PROPOSALS

13   Q.   What is the Company’s stated purpose for proposing Rate Nos. 50

14        and 51 and the Energy Service Agreement?

15   A.   EPE is asking the Commission to approve an entire package for large load

16        customers: the rates a data center would pay, the contracts the data center

17        would sign, and the rules that decide who pays for the lines and substations

18        built for that data center. I refer to all three elements as the Company’s large

19        load proposals. In regard to the rates, EPE proposes two large load tariffs.

20        Rate No. 50 would apply to a customer using at least 30 megawatts at a high



                                             3
                        DOCKET NO. 25-00082-UT
              DIRECT TESTIMONY OF COURTNEY FIELDMAN

 1        load factor. 1 Rate No. 51 would apply to a customer using at least 10

 2        megawatts. 2 However, neither rate can be used until the customer signs a

 3        contract, known as an Energy Services Agreement (“ESA”), to take service

 4        under the new rates, if approved. 3 The Company also asks the Commission

 5        to replace Rule No. 8. That rule determines whether the data center pays for

 6        a new line or a new substation, or whether that cost goes into the rates other

 7        customers pay. 4 CCAE Witness Nelson provides further analysis and

 8        recommendations regarding Rate No. 50, Rate No. 51, and Rule No. 8.

 9   Q.   For the large load proposals, has EPE identified specific loads or

10        customers?

11   A.   EPE has only described a load, but I understand that no large load customers

12        have signed an ESA. 5 The Company states that, at full operation, large load

13        customers such as data centers will be EPE’s largest retail customers, with

14        expected peak loads greater than 30 megawatts and a load factor in excess

15        of 85%. 6 EPE states that it has a potential New Mexico customer requesting

15        would only commit to a twenty-year term.

 1   Q.   Would an ESA filed in the compliance docket provide clarity

 2        regarding the terms between the Company and a large load

 3        customer?

 4   A.   No. EPE only requests that the Commission open a compliance docket in

 5        which it would file the executed ESAs. 12 In response to discovery, EPE said

 6        that public access is subject to the Commission’s case-management rules,

 7        that confidentiality is requested on a case-by-case basis, and that the

 8        agreements will be filed consistent with the terms of the tariffs. 13 If the tariff

 9        does not address the security amount and the ramp quantity, a filing

10        consistent with the tariff would be any amount EPE fills in the blank.

11        Compliance is effectively just filling in the blank. As a ratepayer protection

12        mechanism, this cedes Commission authority to the utility. I am concerned

13        about potential arbitrariness in how EPE applies this ceded discretion.

14                Importantly, filing a fully executed ESA in a compliance docket

15        would not decide whether the added term protects other customers. EPE

16        represents that Section 10 is reserved for any additional terms that may be

17        necessary for or specific to a customer. 14 If the tariff leaves the security

18        amount blank and leaves Section 10 open, a filing consistent with the tariff

 1         can include a security figure and a customer-specific term that was not in

 2         front of the Commission in this case. These amounts would not be

 3         determinable from the tariffs the Commission is asked to approve.

 4         Operating information about a site can be protected. The dollars-per-

 6         an upgrade are the terms that would verify Mr. Novela’s statement that the

 7         ESAs “help[] to ensure fair cost allocation that prevents subsidies.” 15 The

 8         Company’s proposed filing protocol does not supply those terms and makes

 9         EPE’s claim unverifiable.

10   Q.    Do the Commission’s rules provide any relevant requirements for

11         rates and ESAs?

12   A.    Yes. While I am not a lawyer, the Commission’s rules provide requirements

13         for a utility’s filed rates. 16 Specifically, the Commission’s rules require that

14         rate pages include (1) minimum or customer charges and (2) any general or

15         specific conditions, exceptions, or limitations regarding the rate and service

16         provided by the rate. 17 The Commission may reject rates, rules, or forms

 1        that “are not in substantial compliance with Commission rules, orders, or

 2        applicable statutes.” 18

 3   Q.   What do you recommend regarding the Company’s proposed large

 4        load proposals?

 5   A.   I recommend that the Commission require affirmative approval of an ESA.

 6        As CCAE Witness Nelson discusses, the ESA should be approved before it

 7        takes effect. By doing so, the Commission can ensure that the terms of an

 8        ESA—including the security amount, minimum billing provisions, and exit

 9        fee methodology—adequately protect existing customers. CCAE Witness

10        Nelson provides additional recommendations regarding the Company’s

11        large load proposals.

12               III.    EPE’S LOW-INCOME RATE PROPOSAL

13   Q.   Is the Company proposing a low-income rate in this case?

14   A.   Yes. The Company proposes a low-income rider that would waive the

15        residential monthly customer charge for qualifying customers. 19 Recovery

16        would be confined to the residential class only. EPE ties the rider to NMSA

17        1978 § 62-8-6(C), which authorizes low-income rates and programs. 20 The

18        statute authorizes low-income rates and programs; it does not limit the


     18
          Id. § 17.1.210.11(H).
     19
          James Schichtl Direct Test. Am. 20:20–21:1 (Aug. 6, 2026).
     20
          See Novela Direct Am. 56:18–21.

                        DOCKET NO. 25-00082-UT
              DIRECT TESTIMONY OF COURTNEY FIELDMAN

 1        Commission to a customer-charge waiver. A credit that addresses only the

 2        customer charge leaves the larger energy-charge increase, and any residual

 3        large load cost recovered in that charge, unmitigated for low-income

 4        customers.

 5   Q.   Does the low-income rate statute limit the Commission to a customer-

 6        charge waiver?

 7   A.   While I am not a lawyer, I understand that § 62-8-6(C) authorizes the

 8        Commission to approve low-income rates and programs. 21 A credit that

 9        addresses only the customer charge leaves the larger energy-charge increase

10        unmitigated for low-income customers.

11   Q.   How does the Company’s proposed rider compare to the rate increase

12        the Company has proposed?

13   A.   EPE proposes a waiver of the residential customer charge. The proposed

14        credit amount does not offset any other charges, for example, the energy

15        charge. 22 The customer charge would increase from $7.00 to $18.89, so a

16        full waiver would return at most $18.89 per month. In the application, the

17        retail electric rate finds that “at 750 kilowatt-hours in a summer month,

18        which is the average usage level for residential customers, the notice

 1          provides that a residential customer would receive a $55.00 non-fuel

2           increase.” 23 If a qualifying low-income customer took service under the

3           rider as filed, that customer’s new bill would increase substantially despite

4           the credit. The credit does not grow if a later rate case or true-up collects an

5           unpaid large load reservation through the energy charge. A customer-

6           charge-only credit, therefore, leaves any residual large load cost that is

7           recovered in the energy charge unmitigated for low-income customers.

8                   The record requires a comparison between the amount of the

9           customer charge that would be credited and the amount of the rate increase

10          low-income customers would receive if EPE’s proposed rate increases are

11          approved. This comparison appropriately calls for consideration of the

12          effectiveness of EPE’s proposal. While the credit EPE proposes for the LI

13          residential customer could eventually increase, it is currently insufficient to

14          compensate for the massive rate increase EPE is requesting and that rate’s

15          impact on the LI residential customer. Even with the credit, the average low-

16          income ratepayer will experience a $55.00 increase upon full

17          implementation of phase 1 and phase 2 of the proposal.

 1   Q.     Why is it necessary for utilities to have low-income rates?

 2   A.     The cost burdens of energy disproportionately affect the low-income

 3          population. The low-income population is also affected by energy insecurity

 4          at a much higher and dramatic rate than other socio-economic classes or

 5          residential customers.

 6   Q.     What is an energy or cost burden?

 7   A.     Energy burden is the percentage of pretax income spent on utilities. A

 8          household that spends 6 percent or more of pretax income on utilities is

 9          generally considered energy burdened. 24 Recent survey data show that low-

10          income households pay at least 13.3 percent of pretax income on utilities,

11          compared with 2.5 percent for high-income households. 25 This is a

12          noticeable increase from previous survey years. The same survey revealed

13          that among low-income households 53 percent experience energy

14          insecurity, compared with 12 percent of high-income households. 26 A $55

15          monthly non-fuel increase on an average residential bill would increase the

16          energy burden for EPE’s low-income customers.



     24
           Michael Eggleston, Utility Cost Pressures and Energy Insecurity Differ by
     Household Income (Oct. 13, 2026), https://www.stlouisfed.org/on-the-
     economy/2026/oct/utility-cost-pressures-energy-insecurity-differ-household-
     income.

 1   Q.     How does the Company’s proposed rate increase affect energy burdens

 2          for LI households?

 3          Because the proposed credit offsets at most $18.89 of that increase, the net

 4          increase remains large enough to deepen existing burdens or push additional

 5          low-income households above the 6 percent threshold. The proposed rider

 6          does not prevent that outcome, and any additional residual large load cost

 7          recovered in the energy charge would deepen it further.

 8   Q.     What is energy insecurity?

 9   A.     Energy insecurity is the inability to adequately meet household energy

10          needs, and it includes dimensions of economic hardship, physical or

11          structural deficiencies that affect thermal comfort, and coping mechanisms

12          that a household adapts to manage the physical and economic hardships of

13          energy burdens. 27 Energy insecurity occurs when at least one of the

14          following hardships occurs:

15             •   A person in the household forgoes or reduces necessities to pay
16                 utility bills;
17             •   the home may be kept at unsafe or uncomfortable temperatures;
18             •   a household member receives a disconnection notice;
19             •   the household loses utility service due to a shutoff; or,



     27
             Diana Hernandez et al., Columbia Ctr. Global Energy Pol’y, What is
     Energy Insecurity (Oct. 26, 2023),
     https://www.energypolicy.columbia.edu/publications/energy-insecurity-in-the-
     united-states/.


                                            12
                        DOCKET NO. 25-00082-UT
              DIRECT TESTIMONY OF COURTNEY FIELDMAN

 1            •   the heating or cooling equipment is not working. 28

 2        A customer-charge-only credit can increase the likelihood that additional

 3        households will face one or more of these dimensions of energy insecurity.

 4   Q.   Are low-income customers more cost burdened and energy insecure

 5        than other residential customers?

6    A.   Yes. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s

7         Residential   Energy    Consumption     Survey    (“RECS”),   low-income

8         households pay at least 13.3% of pre-tax income on utilities in comparison

9         to high household incomes contributing 2.5% of pre-tax income to utility

10        costs. This is a noticeable increase from previous RECs years. 29 The most

11        recent RECS also revealed that 53% of low-income households experience

12        energy insecurity, and 12% of high-income households also experience

13        energy insecurity. 30

14   Q.   Please explain why crediting the customer charge of $18.89 may not

15        result in savings for the low-income customer?

16   A.   On the one hand, the low-income customer will be credited the customer

17        charge, which will eventually be $18.86. But the low-income residential

 1        customer will be required to pay the full increase in the energy charge.

 2        Based upon this proposal, the average bill will increase by $55.00.

 3   Q.   Why is EPE proposing to increase the proposed customer charge from

 4        $7.00 to $18.86?

 5   A.   EPE says that the changes they propose to the customer charge represent

 6        certain fixed costs that supposedly mitigate the effects caused by low-usage

 7        customers, such as those who are net-metered (have rooftop solar), and that

 8        they are proposing a rate that will more accurately “signal” to customers.

 9        EPE states that “unless fixed costs are recovered through appropriate fixed

10        charges, other customers in the class bear the burden of the fixed costs

11        avoided by customers who install energy efficiency measures, purchase

12        distributed renewable generation or otherwise reduce their energy

13        consumption.” 31 EPE claims that higher-than-average usage customers

14        subsidize lower-than-average usage customers. 32 This proposal, however,

15        reduces price signaling and results in subsidizing high-use customers.

 1   Q.     Are these proposed fixed costs typically included in a customer

 2          charge?

 3   A.     No. The customer charge normally includes only the costs of billing and

 4          collection and is typically levied regardless of electricity usage. 33 As sales

 5          have declined among certain customers, utilities are seeking to include

 6          distribution costs in fixed charges. 34 In addition, this proposed approach is

 7          one that likely results in double allocation of costs to residential customers

 8          and overallocation of costs to low-use customers, such as the low-income

 9          population or those with distributed generation systems, or as EPE provides

10          those who purchase distributed renewable generation, like community

11          solar. 35 New Mexico defines customer charge as the charge that is usually

12          characterized as a customer or monthly service charge, does not vary with

13          the level of usage, and generally includes such costs as administrative,

14          billing, and metering costs. 36

 1   Q.   Is EPE moving costs that have traditionally been included in the per

 2        kWh charge to customer charges?

 3   A.   Yes. EPE is proposing to move some distribution system-related costs from

 4        the energy charge to the customer charge. For example, EPE classifies

 5        “Account No. 369 – Services” as “a customer-related cost and is assigned

6         to the Customer - 369 Services component under Customer.” 37 EPE

7         describes Account No. 369 as “costs of service drop from the distribution

 8        system to serve customers.” 38 Based on the Company’s description, such

 9        costs should be assigned as distribution-related.

10   Q.   Is EPE’s characterization of these costs consistent with the definitions

11        of “customer charge” and “distribution”?

12   A.   No. The Commission’s regulations define distribution as “the delivery of

13        electric power from the transmission system through distribution lines to

14        the meter of the retail customer.” 39 To the extent that the costs of service

15        drops are incurred to deliver electric power from the transmission system

16        through distribution lines to the retail customer’s meter, these costs are not

17        properly included in EPE’s customer charge. I recommend that EPE remove

 1        “Account No. 369 – Services” costs from the customer charge and allocate

 2        and assign them as distribution-related costs.

 3   Q.   Would EPE’s proposed change affect price signaling?

 4   A.   Yes, because while EPE’s overall rate increase is still significant, moving

 5        costs into the customer charge that have traditionally been collected through

 6        the energy charge make it a fixed charge that cannot be reduced by reducing

 7        kWh energy usage. Reducing the portion of the bill that the customer can

 8        control reduces the incentive for consumers to conserve energy (or use less

 9        energy). 40 Another effect is that it shifts large user costs to other users, so

10        that the bill impact means that large users see a reduction in overall charges.

11   Q.   Please explain why this current EPE proposal may not be good for

12        low-income ratepayers.

13   A.   At the end of the day, many low-income ratepayers are low-use customers.

14        A high customer charge creates the illusion of savings, because low-income

15        customers will still pay the higher energy charges that EPE proposes here.

16        Practically speaking, a higher customer charge creates several policy

17        conflicts, too, because it means low-income advocates might advocate for

18        higher credits (in the form of a higher customer charge), but other residential

19        ratepayers will not benefit from the higher charges, creating conflict within


     40
          Lazar, supra, at 3.


                                            17
                        DOCKET NO. 25-00082-UT
              DIRECT TESTIMONY OF COURTNEY FIELDMAN

 1        and among ratepayer advocates. Also, as noted above, very important, the

 2        incentive for energy conservation decreases as customer charges increase.

 3   Q.   Does moving costs into the customer charge affect the incentive to

 4        conserve energy or participate in energy efficiency programs?

 5   A.   Yes. EPE states that unless fixed costs are recovered through appropriate

 6        fixed charges, other customers bear the burden of fixed costs avoided by

 7        customers who install energy efficiency measures or reduce their energy

 8        consumption. 41 The customer charge is defined as a charge that does not

 9        vary with the level of usage and generally includes administrative, billing,

10        and metering costs. 42 When distribution costs that have traditionally been

11        recovered in the energy charge are moved into the customer charge, the per-

12        kilowatt-hour price declines. A lower per-kilowatt-hour price reduces the

13        economic incentive for customers, including low-income customers, to

14        conserve energy or participate in energy efficiency programs. This is known

15        as price elasticity: lower per-kWh prices that result when a significant

16        portion of costs are recovered in a fixed customer charge often stimulate




     41
          Manuel Carrasco Direct Test. Am. 20:4–7 (Aug. 6, 2026).
     42
          § 17.9.531.7 NMAC.


                                          18
                        DOCKET NO. 25-00082-UT
              DIRECT TESTIMONY OF COURTNEY FIELDMAN

 1        energy consumption. 43 The signal differential to “use less energy” becomes

 2        weaker, so customers use more energy. 44

 3               A high customer charge also creates an artificial appearance of

 4        savings for low-income customers who receive the credit, while those

 5        customers continue to pay the higher energy charges. In practice, many low-

 6        income customers are low-use customers; they do not benefit from higher

 7        customer charges, and the design can result in overallocation of costs to

 8        low-use customers, including those with distributed generation. In moving

 9        some distribution system-related costs from the energy charge to the

10        customer charge, the proposed design therefore weakens the price signal

11        that supports efficiency and conservation, which is the same price signal

12        that verified flexibility and virtual power plants rely on to reduce firm

13        capacity need.

14               A high customer charge reduces the economic incentive to save

15        energy. As the cost of a kWh decreases relative to the cost of an energy-

16        efficient practice, it is less likely that a customer will adopt energy

17        efficiency or conservation. This has consequences for incremental utility

18        investment in energy efficiency programs.



     43
          Lazar, supra at 3.
     44
          Id. at 1.

              DIRECT TESTIMONY OF COURTNEY FIELDMAN

1    Q.   Should the low-income rate be dependent upon the customer charge?

2    A.   No, this creates too many conflicts and disturbs the incentives that exist for

3         the low-income customer to conserve energy or participate in energy

4         efficiency programs. While the low-income customer may see the charge

5         credited on their bill, this credit has nothing to do with the customer’s

6         energy use, which has historically been low. Low-income customers are not

7         typically high-energy users. Low-income ratepayers will actually see their

8         bills increase despite the customer charge they could see under this

9         proposal.

10   Q.   Does EPE’s proposal shield the low-income customer from increased

11        bills?

12   A.   Not really. While it may appear significant to credit the entire customer

DAC 5-4.

       Are the rates proposed for Rate 50 and Rate 51 designed to collect all expected costs to
       serve future customers that may be served by these rate classes? If not, please answer the
       following:

           A.   What costs are not included?
           B.   How will those costs be collected?
           C.   Who will pay for those costs?

RESPONSE:

       Please see objections. Without waiving these objections, El Paso Electric Company
       ("EPE") responds as follows:

           No. The rates proposed for Rate 50 and Rate 51 are designed to collect the Company’s
           cost of service allocated to those rate classes. If the Commission approves EPE’s
           proposed cost-based rates, customers taking service under Rates 50 and 51 will be
           charged rates designed to recover the costs allocated to those classes.

           A.   The costs of any customer-dedicated facilities are not included in the base rates
                proposed for Rates 50 and 51.
           B.   Those costs will be collected through a Facility Charge, as described in the
                tariffed Facility Charge provision of the proposed Rate 50 and 51 rate schedules.
           C.   The customer which is served by the customer-dedicated facilities will pay for
                those costs through the Facility Charge.
